name: Ann Trowbridge
text: The proposed arch is an ugly, garish design. It is too tall, a waste of current and future taxpayers' money and will permanently scar the federal landscape of both Arlington and Washington. If allowed to be built by this commission, my hope is it would be immediately removed by the next administration. As we know, Trump's new rule says a president can demolish what he wants of federal buildings and landscape without Congressional approval or commission review.

name: Fran Bowman
text: I oppose the construction of any type of "monumental arch". This design is ugly, it is grandiose, it is unoriginal, and it just gets in the way. What is it a monument of, other than the failed Trump presidency? The survival of our republic for 250 years is enough of a monument for me.

name: Jane Allison
text: Please don't build this monstrous vanity project to please Trump. No one wants it or his billion dollar ballroom. He is destroying the beautiful city of Washington, DC with monuments to himself. The people used to have a say in this. Trump doesn't get to spend taxpayer money and junk up the city any way he wants.

name: Maryanne Berry
text: Thank you for the opportunity to voice my total opposition to this ill-conceived and garish arch. When Veterans groups, historians, architects and other with actual artistic expertise tell you it is a huge mistake, please listen. It is reminiscent of regimes that are the complete opposite of The United States and its values. NO to the arch.

text: This preposterous arch needs Congressional approval and funding prior to any approvals by this Commission! This is another example of authoritarianism by this corrupt administration! There is no funding allocated and the Congress has not reviewed or considered this monstrosity! It will devastate the views from Arlington to the Lincoln Memorial. name: Natasha Seaman
text: This arch is way too big for its location. It does nothing for the National Mall, and it obstructs the view of the Mall from Arlington Cemetery. Triumphal arches are not meant to be so monumental in scale. As a symbol, it does not have significance in our country, especially for the younger generation. This is a huge waste of money and only serves one man's ego.

name: Christopher Wilson
text: Dear NCPC, I am writing to object to the grandiose scale of the proposed "New Monumental Arch". Whist I agree that it is it a good idea to create a monument that celebrates the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States, I do NOT agree that its proposed 250-feet height (including top sculpture) is appropriate. Even without the sculpture, the arch's proposed 166 feet would be equally inappropriate, dwarfing the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial next door. Please do not approve this outlandish proposal. Thanking you for your time, Dr. Christopher S. Wilson Architecture and Design Historian Ringling College of Art + Design Sarasota, Florida, USA cwilson@c.ringling.edu

name: Katharine Wells
text: Dear NCPC, I write to express my deepest objection to the "New Monumental Arch" (aka, the Arc de Trump), which is entirely out of character with our nation's historical tradition of monument building. It is galling that this arch is such a blatant monument to President Trump, rather than to the 250th anniversary of the nation as a whole as Trump sometimes claims. Indeed, he has frankly admitted that the arch is a monument to himself, as when we was asked whom it was for, he said "me." It is unprecedented for a sitting president to initiate a monument to himself. Trump should wait for his legacy to be determined in the fullness of time, and if the citizens of this country wish to create a monument to him after a suitable length of time has elapsed since his presidency, then they will do so. But beginning this controversial monument now will only create future embarrassment and expense, as there will be many calls to halt or reverse its construction, or to demolish it if it is completed. I grew up in Washington, DC, and I have driven through the proposed site for the arch countless times. I have no objection to a monument being built there, nor do I object to the blocking of sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial and the Robert E. Lee Memorial (since I do not feel General Lee warrants a memorial that is visible from the National Mall). But I do strongly object to using the semiquincentennial as a pretext for memorializing a sitting president. Doing so is a betrayal of our nation's great historical traditions of democratic commemoration. I ask that you do not allow this project to go ahead as proposed. Thanking you for your time, K. L. H. Wells Associate Professor Department of Art History University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee

name: Sue Leonard
text: Just because other countries have arches, does not mean we need or want one. We definitely do not need one of the size the president wants. It's gaudy, it's too large, its location is sketchy for something of that weight and will obstruct views that carry meaning for many of us. The fact that he wants it to be taller than the Lincoln Memorial is beyond offensive. To quote Nancy Reagan, just say no. I'm tired of sycophants yielding to the whims of an insecure autocrat who's already lining his pockets with taxpayer dollars.

name: Cristelle Baskins
text: The proposed "Monumental Arch" is a monumental waste of taxpayer money. This kind of egotistical display is reminiscent of Mussolini, Kim Jong Il, or Saddam Hussein. Like everything else Trump designs, it will be tacky, out of scale, and an unnecessary addition to the Washington DC landscape. He's already destroyed the Rose Garden, the East Wing of the White House (without clearing it through Historic Preservation or Planning), painted the reflecting pool an artificial blue, and added his name to public buildings where it doesn't belong. This is the WASTE, FRAUD, and CORRUPTION that Trump claims to see everywhere except in his own out-of-control spending. But of course, this committee was hand-picked to rubber stamp all of this nonsense. It will be up to the next administration to tear it all down and return some dignity to our capital. That day cannot come soon enough.

name: Laura McBride
text: Please please please no arch. It's gigantic, expensive, stupid looking, and completely out of character for Washington, DC. It will also ruin the site line between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, a view that is supposed to represent the national unity that came after the Civil War. I'm aware national unity is at a low point, but that is not something that deserves a triumphal arch. Also it would add more chaos to an already overwhelmingly busy traffic area and create a hazard for pedestrians trying to reach it. Also, I am writing to protest the proposal to replace the tragically destroyed East Wing of the White House with an enormous ballroom. The recent demolition was carried out without proper consent or comprehensive planning, demonstrating a blatant disregard for both process and the historic significance of the structure. Replacing it with a disproportionately massive ballroom would disrupt the architectural harmony of the White House and create a huge eyesore. I strongly urge the Commission to reject any proposal for an arch and to require that any construction plans be carefully reviewed and fully approved through the appropriate channels before any work continues on the East Wing of the White House. Preservation of the White House as the people's house must take precedence over the desired grandeur or spectacle of it's current occupant. We cannot allow the dignity of this nation to be compromised by expensive, enormous, ill-considered, tacky, monuments that are only one man's attempt to aggrandize himself.

name: James Smailes
text: Comments on Triumphal Arch Comments may have been submitted previously on the inappropriateness of the size and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, but my comments concern the increased danger to traffic that will result from its construction. As a Professional Transportation Engineer (P.E.), I am very concerned about the obstructed vision for drivers that will result from construction of the Arch. It will create two massive walls approximately 186 feet wide by 110 feet deep, and very high, blocking drivers' vision as they approach the circle. One will be able to see through the Arch at times, but much of the drivers' vision will be restricted, which is the worst thing to do in a Round About. The approaching roads are confusing and require careful merging to enter the circle safely. Just how the massive walls will hinder drivers' vision can be seen in presentation Slides 7, 8, and 15. Memorial Circle is approximately 300 feet in diameter, but the width of the arch is more than half the diameter of the circle. The restricted vision will lead to slower traffic, more congestion, and potentially more accidents as traffic volumes increase. To summarize, the arch is far too big for the space, will obstruct view sheds as shown in the other presentation slides, and could lead to increased congestion, pollution, and more accidents. Thank you for considering this, James A. Smailes, P.E.

name: Meg Cowan
text: I strongly oppose NCPC File No. 8778, the proposed New Monumental Arch on Memorial Avenue in Washington, DC. This proposal should be rejected outright. It is unnecessary, grotesquely self-serving, and completely inappropriate for one of the most solemn and historically significant landscapes in the United States. Memorial Avenue, Arlington Memorial Bridge, the Lincoln Memorial, and the approach to Arlington National Cemetery already carry deep national meaning. This proposed arch is a disgusting self-aggrandizement to Donald Trump, a president who deserves no monument, no shrine, and no taxpayer-supported tribute to stoke his ego. Public land in Washington, DC belongs to the American people. It should never be used to glorify one man, especially in a location so closely tied to sacrifice, service, mourning, and national memory. Placing a vanity arch in this setting would be a slap in the face to all Americans, especially the service members buried at Arlington National Cemetery and the families who go there to honor them. That landscape deserves dignity, restraint, and reverence. It should not be turned into a stage set for Trump's ego. The historic spaces in Washington, DC belong to the nation. This proposal cheapens the setting, overwhelms the existing landscape, and turns a solemn public place into a political trophy. I urge the Commission to reject this concept and protect the integrity of Memorial Avenue, Arlington Memorial Bridge, Arlington National Cemetery, and the surrounding monumental core.

name: Stacie Grove
text: Arch To Whom It May Concern, I am writing in strong opposition to the proposed "Arc de Trump" monument project in Washington, D.C. Our nation's capital is home to memorials that commemorate extraordinary moments in American history and individuals whose contributions have stood the test of time. These spaces are meant to reflect broad national unity, sacrifice, leadership, and historical significance evaluated through the perspective of generations — not the passions and divisions of current politics. Fast-tracking a monumental tribute to a deeply polarizing contemporary political figure undermines the integrity and dignity of our national civic spaces. Regardless of political affiliation, Americans should be concerned about setting a precedent in which enormous monuments are created to elevate living or recently serving political personalities before history has had the opportunity to assess their legacies fairly and objectively. I am also deeply troubled by the priorities reflected in this proposal. Whether funded directly by taxpayers or through wealthy private donors with political interests, this project represents a staggering misuse of influence, resources, and public attention at a time when our country faces urgent needs involving infrastructure, education, housing insecurity, veterans' services, environmental protection, and public health. Washington, D.C. should not become a stage for oversized displays of personal glorification. Our national monuments should inspire reflection, humility, service, sacrifice, and unity — not political branding or personality cults. I respectfully urge decision-makers, planning commissions, preservation boards, and elected officials to reject this proposal and preserve the historical and civic integrity of our nation's capital for future generations. Sincerely, Stacie Grove

name: Anne Pagano
text: Dear Mr. Acosta, Mr. Scharf, and Distinguished Members of the Commission: I write to submit my formal opposition to the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle, referenced as CFA 21/MAY/26-1. While I recognize the worthy impulse to commemorate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I respectfully but firmly oppose this project on three substantive grounds. FIRST: INAPPROPRIATE PROXIMITY TO ARLINGTON NATIONAL CEMETERY Arlington National Cemetery is hallowed ground — a place of solemn mourning, reverence, and national memory. The experience of visiting our fallen heroes demands an atmosphere of quiet dignity, free from monumental intrusion. Placing a 250-foot triumphal arch at the entrance to that sacred space would fundamentally alter the character of the surrounding landscape and diminish the gravity that every visitor to the Cemetery deserves to feel. No celebratory monument, however well-intentioned, should compete with the solemn purpose of honoring those who gave their lives in service to this nation. SECOND: OBSTRUCTION OF EXISTING VIEWS AND NATIONAL VISTAS The ceremonial corridor between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House represents one of the most deliberately designed and symbolically significant vistas in the United States. This axis was conceived to represent post-Civil War national reconciliation and unity. A 250-foot structure at Memorial Circle would obstruct and disrupt these historic sightlines, cluttering a landscape that has served Americans and visitors from around the world with clarity and meaning for over a century. The Commission bears a responsibility to protect these irreplaceable visual relationships, not diminish them in the name of new construction. THIRD: THE DESIGN UNDERMINES THE STRENGTH AND DIGNITY APPROPRIATE TO AN AMERICAN NATIONAL MONUMENT American national monuments have long been distinguished by their boldness, solemnity, and classical strength. The addition of golden winged figures and ornate cornice work at the top of the proposed arch introduces a decorative quality that is at odds with this tradition. Rather than projecting the strong, enduring character that our monuments are known for, the proposed crown of the arch conveys an aesthetic of ornamentation over gravitas. I urge the Commission to reject this design element and, more broadly, to reconsider whether this project in its current form — in its proposed location and with its current design — is worthy of the landscape it would permanently occupy. For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Commission to deny approval of the proposed Triumphal Arch as currently designed and sited. Should the concept of a commemorative arch be revisited in the future, I encourage the Commission to consider an alternative location that does not intrude upon the solemnity of Arlington National Cemetery or compromise the historic vistas of our National Mall. Thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments. I trust the Commission will weigh them with the seriousness this matter deserves. Respectfully submitted, Anne S. Pagano

name: Nancy Bailey Stone
text: My parents are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. My father died in 1962. I can see the Kennedy memorial from the grave site (my mother was inurned in 1998). I can see that eternal flame which brings comfort to me. The thought that if I turn around, I will be confronted by that monstrosity that is being proposed fills me with grief, with outrage, and with anger. No one should have to experience the desecration of their loved one's grave in such a heinous fashion. When my parents were buried at Arlington, I had the consolation that, in perpetuity, their burial place would be one of care and a place where others would find solace. The homage to a man who received multiple deferrals from serving during the war in Vietnam is a disgrace to the men and women in the armed forces who are buried at Arlington. He has no respect for them on any level. I am angry and frustrated that despite the opposition to this abomination, that the sycophants on this commission approve the plans. Each of you will have to live with this decision on your conscience.

name: John Hayes
text: As an architect, I urge you to reject this scheme which contradicts the plan made by the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission and approved by Congress Proposing to build two columns on Columbia Island, the Commission made clear that they should be placed to frame the view of the Lincoln Memorial and not to block that view. To that end, they proposed placing the columns about 300 feet apart - about 150 feet to either side of the axis from the Lincoln Memorial to the Cemetery entrance, the Lee Mansion, and the grave of L'Enfant. 0n page 9 of the report, the Commission said: "Being so intimately related to the bridge, it was thought proper that the plans for the ultimate development of Columbia Island as a park should be included as part of the project for the Memorial Bridge.Accordingly, the lines of the shore of the island have been somewhat rectified to. permit a cross axis almost perpendicular to the main axis of the bridge and extending the full length of the island The intersection of these two axes has suggested a plaza with fitting architectural adornment in a measure supplemental to the Lincoln Memorial across the river, and for this purpose two stately columns are proposed to be erected here, framing in but not interfering with the view of the Lincoln Memorial from the direction of the Lee Mansion. These columns symboli surmounted by statues of Victory, the stylobates whence they rise offering surfaces suitable for decorations, bas-relief, and inscriptions. The columns are 166 feet high, or practically of the same height as the Colonne de Juillet in Paris." The critical point here is: "Framing in but not interfering with the view of the Lincoln Memorial from the direction of the Lee Mansion" Putting an "Arc de Triomphe" on the axis of the bridge is not justified by the two widely-spaced columns in the 1920's report. It will "interfere with the view of the Lincoln Memorial" which is precisely what the original report said was to be avoided Nor will seeing isolated bits and snatches through the opening in the arch accomplish what the Commission design proposed and Congress approved. John Hayes, FAIA P.S. The Commission report is available at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-08240_00_00-002-0095-0000/pdf/ The plan from which I scaled the "about 300 feet" spacing of the columns follows page 51. A rendering showing the columns in elevation view is between pages 34 and 35.

name: Alexandra DeCandia
text: Dear Chairman Scharf and NCPC Commissioners: I urge you to reject the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle and urge the administration to follow the laws that have kept this landscape protected and celebrated for decades. The administration has not completed the process required by the Commemorative Works Act for placing a monument in Area I of the monumental core. It has not completed environmental review under NEPA. It has not completed historic preservation consultation under Section 106. And it does not have the approval of Congress and the American public. This 250-foot structure would permanently transform the view from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, one of the most sacred landscapes in America, where families visit fallen veterans every day. Once that view is gone, it is gone forever. Rushing this project to meet a political deadline is not a reason to skip required legal and environmental reviews. Please require full legal compliance before this project moves one step further. Thank you,

text: RE: New Monumental Arch (also known as United States Triumphal Arch and Independence Arch) NCPC File Number 8778 I am writing to ask you to decline the proposal for this New Monumental Arch. name: Mary Brush
text: Monumental design is a process of discussion, iteration, proportion, and aesthetic. Within all of that is the layers of meaning and message. Processes exist to design, refine, present and obtain consensus. This processes have not been followed and the presented design is reflective of that. These designs are hasty. The proportions are out of balance. Does the committee want to be part of something that is immediately dated to a quick decision but no substance. The grand arches that are admired as inspiration for this project were not approved of and constructed with great speed to complete within an election cycle. Great work. Great admiration and great monuments take time. The NPS and GSA and monument committees with experts in architecture, public place, and the power of commemoration exist and deserve a true seat at the table. Approval by donor buddies is not a way to achieve the intended monumental adoration.

name: Diana Thatcher
text: Dear Commissioners, I stand in strong opposition to the planned monumental arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Our nation's capital represents our long-term history and reflects the American people, not a short-lived administration. Please consider the implications of this object and how it will be viewed by future generations. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Diana Thatcher

name: Charity Bedoy
text: To the National Capital Planning Commission: I respectfully request that any proposal involving a large-scale commemorative structure be evaluated using consistent standards focused on historical significance, long-term public value, fiscal impact, and effects on civic space. Large monuments and memorial structures often become lasting parts of the national landscape for generations. Because of that, careful consideration should be given to questions such as: * What public purpose does the project serve? * What are the projected construction, maintenance, and security costs over time? * How would the project affect surrounding public spaces, infrastructure, and visitor use? * Does the proposal align with established principles and precedents for commemorative works? * How will the project contribute to the broader character and shared civic identity of the capital region? I encourage the Commission to ensure that any decision reflects long-term planning considerations, historical context, and broad public interest. Thank you for your consideration.

The intent is clear and unequivocal in the design. We, as a nation must keep the original and profound intention of the design of these hallowed places as they are. The final rest of thousands of our most heroic soldiers from all walks of life, who laid down their lives in order to perpetuate our Union, face the grave and solemn leader who spent his last breaths trying to sew up the near fatal wound to our "experiment." The legacy of Abraham Lincoln and what the Civil War means to our history is so much more than any leader since, and must be honored in visible ways for all generations moving this nation forward to see. These two places must remain in the line of sight, much alike to the planning to have Grant in line with Lincoln. The only amendments to such treasures of our past must be done by non-partisan committees who have the experience and historical perspective to improve upon the memorials or manage their upkeep. No sitting president should have a single inkling to change these places, nor erect new ones to glorify themselves, ultimately at the expense of the People of this country. name: David Klinger
text: Dear Sir: I was a resident of the District of Columbia from 1977-1978 and an employee of the U.S. Department of the Interior in Washington, D.C. between 1977 and 1988. I returned many times to Washington during the course of my 35-year career in Washington. In regard to the proposed Triumphal Arch at the gate of Arlington National Cemetery that now comes before you for review, I have been unable to locate in the record for this project any meaningful analysis of the potential impact of this project on the continued line-of-sight between the Eternal Flame in Arlington Cemetery that sits atop the gravesite of President John F. Kennedy and the City of Washington to the east. As you undoubtedly are aware, the location of the Kennedy burial site beneath the Custis-Lee Mansion in Arlington Cemetery was specifically fixed because of President Kennedy's prior examination of the site prior to his untimely death in 1963. That sight affords a direct and unobstructed view between the national cemetery and Washington, across the Memorial Bridge. That line-of-sight was the principal criteria by which an Eternal Flame was conceived and positioned so that it would always remain visible across the Potomac River, when the light was temporarily placed at the time of burial and later, when it was permanently installed. Consult the public records and the popular media of 1963 and you will quickly determine that it was the intent of the Kennedy Family, as well as the management of Arlington National Cemetery, for the Eternal Flame to remain a permanent and unobstructed feature of the landscape in this area. As a commuter by bicycle between downtown Washington and my residence in Arlington, Virginia, across the Memorial Bridge in all seasons and weather, the Eternal Flame served as a faithful and constant beacon in the distance. Cross Memorial Bridge today in the twilight and you will still see that pinpoint of light emanating from Arlington Cemetery, as was intended to be a permanent feature emanating at nighttime from national cemetery since 1963. The record for the proposed project before you fails to address this aspect of heritage in the Nation's Capital. It includes no substantive analysis of the existing line-of-sight between the Eternal Flame and Washington nor any comprehensive predictive model concerning how the proposed Triumphal Arch will obscure or otherwise blot out this permanent feature of the cemetery and its heritage. It has been ignored, overlooked, or missed in the application for this ambitious and massive project. Until such analysis is performed, I submit that the application before you is deficient and that any action by the National Capital Planning Commission should be suspended until such deficiency is remedied. David Klinger 35 Sycamore Lane Lexington, Virginia 540/414-5124 5/26/26

The arch will shatter the calm, quiet atmosphere of Arlington Cemetery and the approach to it from every direction. It is not needed to celebrate or commemorate any of this country's triumphs - there are monuments to all the wars in Washington and throughout the nation. And it is utterly foreign to the memory of the men and women buried there who fought in those wars because of their dedication to our founding principles, not for posthumous glory. The arch will also destroy the landscape of Washington DC because it is so completely out of scale with all of the other important landmarks in the city. I lived in Washington for more than 50 years, and visited Arlington many, many times - even before my parents were buried there. The flat, roundabout approach to the cemetery is the last opportunity for a visitor to take a deep breath before entering the hallowed ground of Arlington Cemetery. Please do not mutilate our nation's capital with this arch.

name: Sarah Saar
text: Dear Members, I write in strong opposition to the proposed monumental arch in Washington, DC. This proposal is wasteful, divisive, and fundamentally at odds with the public interest. At a time when the nation faces serious fiscal pressures, it is indefensible to devote enormous resources to a grandiose monument honoring a man whose leadership many Americans associate with deep national division, rising debt, reckless decision-making, and repeated public disappointment. Washington's monumental landscape should reflect the highest and most enduring national ideals. It should not be used to glorify vanity, reward controversy, or impose a deeply polarizing political statement on the American public. A project of this scale and cost demands broad civic consensus and historical seriousness. This proposal has neither. The expense alone should disqualify it. Americans should not be asked to accept the financial burden of an extravagant symbolic structure when there are far more urgent national priorities. A monumental arch is not a necessity. It is a display of excess. I urge the Commission to reject this proposal outright. The capital deserves planning guided by restraint, dignity, fiscal responsibility, and genuine public purpose—not spectacle built around a single contemporary political figure. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Sarah Saar Sellersburg, IN

name: Arun Baheti
text: The NCPC should decline to approve this project, for reasons that precede any question of design, aesthetics, or historic impact: it is almost certainly unlawful, and it may be dangerous. The law has not been followed. The Commemorative Works Act of 1986 is unambiguous. Congress prohibited the construction of new commemorative works in the District of Columbia and its environs without specific congressional authorization. The planned location at Memorial Circle sits within Lady Bird Johnson Park, designated under "Area I" of the Commemorative Works Act, which carries the strictest congressional oversight. That authorization has not been obtained. The administration's claim that a 1924 congressional resolution suffices is not credible -- a century-old authorization for a conceptually different structure cannot substitute for the specific approval the CWA requires. A coalition of lawmakers has filed an amicus brief in federal court arguing the project violates the Act, and Vietnam War veterans have sued, alleging Congress has not authorized the arch and that required environmental and historic reviews have not been completed. The NCPC should not approve a project currently being litigated on the ground that it is unlawful. Section 106 review has not been completed. The National Historic Preservation Act mandates that Section 106 review be completed prior to project approval. It has not been initiated. This is not a formality -- it is a statutory prerequisite. The FAA question has not been answered. A 250-foot structure in the flight path approaching Reagan National Airport raises serious aviation safety concerns that have not been reviewed. This is not a hypothetical. The January 2025 collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people and prompted a sweeping federal investigation into aviation safety procedures surrounding the busy D.C. airspace. The NTSB found not one single factor but many errors and systemic failures, criticizing the FAA for longstanding failures involving helicopter traffic routes and airspace management. Congress is currently legislating fixes. Introducing a 250-foot permanent obstruction into that same corridor -- without FAA review -- would be reckless under any circumstances. In the current moment, it is unconscionable. The Commission of Fine Arts voted to approve a design. It cannot vote away the law. The NCPC should table this proposal until Congress authorizes it, Section 106 review is completed, and the FAA has fully evaluated the aviation safety implications. In other words: until this project is actually legal, and demonstrably safe.

name: Lynne Mofenson
text: I am horrified by the proposed Monumental Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway, near Arlington National Cemetery. The location of the proposed Arch will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. In addition, the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery, which is the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. The Arlington Cemetery is distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones and serves as a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. I am particularly horrified by the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. I urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." We would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. The project has not been approved by Congress and this work will clearly encroach on Arlington Cemetary and will not protect open space - will actually DECREASE open space. I urge this proposal be disapproved.

name: Ilene Feinman
text: Thank you for the opportunity to register public comment regarding the New Monumental Arch. I wish to register my opposition to the creation of this arch given the below significant concerns. The location of the proposed Arch will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscapes in Washington, D.C., the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. It is because this viewshed carries so much meaning to the country that the National Trust has raised concerns about the proposed Monumental Arch, whose scale, location, and design will disrupt this important visual and symbolic vista. In addition, the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. The critical symbolic importance of the area as it is currently configured demands respect and invites us to contemplate the great significance of our shared American story.

name: Bruce Rieder
text: The proposed arch is the wrong design, the wrong scale, in the wrong place, with the wrong symbolism for the monumental environment of our nation's capital. Every monument, memorial, and institutional federal building is placed for a reason, with a message, respecting its surroundings, and hierarchy. This proposed arch violates every one of those symbolic connections asserting a significance far beyond its substance. There has been no cogent explanation by the applicant as to what triumph this arch is intended to represent. What does it mean in the context of our nation's history? What compelling idea or ideal does it convey? What is the applicant's intention of what message the viewer takes away from the experience of this structure? None of these questions are addressed by the applicant in any convincing way. It seems to be just a "pretty" bauble that we must have because other cities have one. My own impression of the placement and design of this structure is its glorification of white Christian nationalism as a defining idea of our nation's history. The primary view to and through the arch perfectly frames the Robert E. Lee Memorial a.k.a. Arlington House. Immediately above that view are the inscribed words that suggest an incorrect Christian foundation of our nation topped by a golden winged victory figure. This is not "lady liberty" representing none of the qualities of the quiet strength, grace, and humility of that mythic figure that represents the triumph of common people. The gaudy winged victory is an entirely different and inappropriate symbology. The Lincoln Memorial is minimized in this design and placement of the arch. This design says "triumph of white Christian nationalism" to me in its symbology. Finally, as a resident of Arlington, I have frequently travelled that area at night. As anyone who makes that trip knows, the solemn flickering light of the eternal flame at the JFK gravesite is frequently visible in the darkness as one travels across Memorial Bridge. That quiet stirring experience will be completely obliterated by the bulk of the arch as well as by its nighttime lighting in yet one more insult by this applicant to our veteran President John F. Kennedy. For these reasons, I vehemently oppose this proposal as inappropriate.

text: I object to this massive, expensive and overbearing project on the line-of-sight between Arlington Cemetery's Eternal Flame, which marks the gravesite of President John F. Kennedy and was intended to remain perpetually visible across the Potomac in the City of Washington. I have lived in this area for 70 yers and remember when President Kennedy was laid to rest here. The Eternal Flame has been a constant and permanent feature of the Washington-to-Arlington landscape for the past 63 years. Cross the Memorial Bridge tonight, at twilight, and you will still the flame from the gravesite of an assassinated president. It now appears to be threatened by a project of great mass and considerable impact on the surrounding landscape, lacking sufficient consideration for the sacred space that Arlington National Cemetery embodies. There has been NO substantive analysis in the public record that addresses the aspect of the Eternal Flame and its intent when originally conceived. Nor does it take into account the site line to the Custis Lee Mansion and the cemetary, itself. Apparently this little point-of-light, site line has been missed, overlooked, or simply ignored by the current occupant of the White House. And since most of you are just lap dogs, I have little hope that any public comments will be given consideration - just as you ignored the public comments on the gross and hideous tear down of the East Wing. Until this serious oversight is remedied, I submit that the project before the National Capital Planning Commission is deficient and that it cannot act until this point is addressed.

name: Kenneth Kukovich
text: May 26, 2026 FROM: Kenneth M. Kukovich 12602 Trillium Glen Lane Lovettsville, VA 20180 TO: Mr. Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., Chair U.S. Commission of Fine Arts 401 F Street, NW, Suite 312 Washington, DC 20001 Re: CFA 21/MAY/26-1 Memorial Circle, George Washington Memorial Parkway, Washington, DC. New Monumental Arch. Revised Concept. Dear Mr. Cook: As a private citizen and frequent visitor to our nation's capital, I wish to submit the following comments in opposition to the proposed new "monumental arch." First, this proposed arch would not comply with the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." Second, and obviously, it destroys the view from the Lincoln Memorial across the Memorial Bridge to the National Cemetery. As a veteran, I find it extremely distasteful to alter that view. And historically, that view was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. The proposed arch would interfere – destroy – all that. Third, the size is unreasonable. It would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial. It would simply look out of place compared to the current long, open and uninterrupted view across the Bridge. And finally, as a veteran, I am insulted by the way that this arch would degrade our National Cemetery. It would be perceived as an affront to all veterans. I encourage you to reject this proposal – for all Americans. Respectfully, Kenneth M. Kukovich

name: Penny Flavin
text: I am writing to formally express my strong opposition to the proposed monument arch project currently under consideration. While I deeply respect the intent to honor American history, I believe this project is misguided for several important reasons: First, the financial climate does not support this expenditure. At a time when American families and small businesses are facing significant economic hardship, allocating taxpayer funds to a large-scale decorative monument is fiscally irresponsible and tone-deaf to the struggles many citizens are enduring. Second, this project is simply not a necessity. The National Mall already features some of the most iconic and beloved monuments in the world. Additional infrastructure of this nature does not serve a meaningful public need and does not justify the cost. Third, and perhaps most critically, the proposed arch risks obstructing the sightlines and visual integrity of existing monuments that have stood for generations. These structures are part of our shared national heritage, and any construction that diminishes the experience of visiting them should be carefully reconsidered — if not abandoned entirely. I urge decision-makers to prioritize the responsible use of public funds, preserve the existing character of our national landmarks, and redirect these resources toward initiatives that provide tangible benefit to the American people. Thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments.

(And topped, of course, in yet more gold.) While tastes inevitably differ, Donald Trump's is stunningly out of step with all that has gone before - and it has been inflicted on all of us with no appreciation or recognition of our joint heritage. This area was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south. The proposed arch would disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted views that were thoughtfully engineered years ago, and overwhelm the entry to Arlington National Cemetery, where our nation's heroes and heroines have been laid to rest. In addition, the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. text: I write in opposition to the vanity project proposed by the Trump administration creating a monumental arch that will obscure the view of Arlington Cemetery. name: Cindy Langston
text: May 27, 2026 Re: Memorial Circle, George Washington Memorial Parkway, Washington, DC. New Monumental Arch My name is Cindy Langston and I am a resident of the state of Kentucky. I respectfully submit the following comments concerning the current proposal by the Executive Office of the President and the U.S. Department of the Interior to construct a new Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. I urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." I would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. I am also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission itself. We urge the Commission members to await the Section 106 process, which has not yet been initiated. I come from a very long line of military members and feel great honor and pride at the service they have provided to our country. Let us please continue to show our respect for the sacrifices that have been given to our country and honor the women and men who have made the ultimate sacrifice. Thank you for considering my views on this historic matter. Sincerely, Cindy Langston

name: Chris Tully
text: I strongly urge that you disallow the planned large arch near the Arlington Bridge. This structure will block the historically important view between Arlington Cemetery, Arlington House and the Lincoln Memorial. The Capital was purposely designed to provide focus on historic sights and I am opposed to changes driven by the whims of one. text: I am horrified by the idea of this arch. It's scale and location deliberately try to trivialize the Lincoln Memorial and its connection to Arlington National Cemetery. This administration is deliberately ignorant of our nation's history and the importance of the Civil War in the creation of our national character. The arch is a crass, vulgur waste of money. name: Mary Kay Trail
text: This is unnecessary expense and not in line with the other monuments that are there. It will detract and overshadow and is a complete waste of money. Stop this nonsense and do not build this.

name: Laura Hofmann
text: I am writing to urge you to oppose the proposed Triumphal Arch near Arlington Memorial Bridge and Memorial Circle. This project poses an irreversible threat to one of the most historically and symbolically significant landscapes in the United States. The planned location sits at the heart of a profound national viewshed — the visual and symbolic axis connecting the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. This vista was intentionally designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south. It is not merely scenic; it is a carefully considered expression of national unity and healing. No new structure should be permitted to sever that connection. At 250 feet tall, the proposed arch would dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and overwhelm the long, open sightlines that define this part of Washington. It would obstruct the entry to Arlington National Cemetery — the hallowed resting place of over 400,000 veterans and their families, a place that stands as one of the most powerful reminders of American military sacrifice and service. These veterans deserve an unobstructed, dignified approach to their resting place, not a towering arch blocking the view. The public has spoken clearly. During the Commission of Fine Arts' May 2026 hearing, commissioners were told that 99.5% of the more than 600 public comments submitted opposed this structure. I urge the NCPC to honor that overwhelming public sentiment. Preserving Washington's monumental landscape is not about resisting change — it is about protecting the civic and historical meaning embedded in this city's design. The National Trust for Historic Preservation has raised serious concerns about this project's scale, location, and design for exactly these reasons, and I stand with them. I respectfully urge the Commission to reject this proposal and protect the irreplaceable character of our Nation's Capital.

name: Amy Miller
text: Do not review this project because it has not completed its section 106 review. name: Ruth Parr
text: I strongly oppose the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle and urge the Commission to reject this inappropriate and self-serving proposal. Washington's monumental core and Arlington National Cemetery are sacred national spaces meant to honor the sacrifices, service, and memory of Americans who came before us — not to serve as stages for political vanity projects tied to living presidents or current administrations. Monuments of this scale and symbolism should emerge from broad national consensus and historical perspective over time, not from the ambitions or image-building efforts of those currently in power. The proposed Arch would permanently damage one of the most important symbolic landscapes in the United States. Its massive height and scale would overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, obstruct the historic relationship between Arlington Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, and intrude upon the solemn character of Arlington National Cemetery. The simplicity, dignity, and quiet reverence of Arlington stand in direct contrast to the oversized and triumphalist nature of this proposal. At a time when Americans are struggling with rising costs, housing affordability, infrastructure needs, veterans' care, and other pressing national priorities, the Administration should focus on helping the American people rather than pursuing grandiose monument projects designed to elevate political legacy and spectacle. The proposal also appears to be advancing before completion of the legally required Section 106 historic preservation review process. That alone should halt further consideration until full public consultation and preservation review are completed. This proposal is historically inappropriate, visually destructive, fiscally irresponsible, and fundamentally inconsistent with the purpose and character of the nation's most sacred commemorative spaces. It should be rejected in its entirety.

name: Kara White
text: I agree with the following comments by National Trust for Historic Preservation and implore you to reconsider the height, scope and location of this project.: "The proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. We are a nation born of a revolution that freed us from rule by monarchs. As we near our 250th anniversary, I find it especially important to be reminded of, and for us to honor, the history under which our great Nation and Constitution was founded. It is a time for us to come together in a celebration of the ideals that formed this Nation and abide by those principles.

name: Lori Savoie
text: The Arch does not need to be in this location. It will change and misconstrue the significance of the sites already designed for that area. name: Deborah McFalone

name: Tim Baldwin
text: This is another crass desecration of our nation's capitol. First the Rose Garden, then the East Wing, then the Reflecting Pool, and now this? name: Marie Allen
text: The concept and location of this monumental arch are faulty. The cost is prohibitive especially as Americans are having personal financial challenges. name: Nancy Barnes
text: I oppose building the monumental arch. This arch would block Arlington Cemetery and the Lincoln memorial, which I believe might be their plan. The National Mall was designed over many years with years of planning for each addition. This is sacrilege. This is a desecration of the People's rights and an area viewed by many as honored ground. I have visited Washington DC only twice in my life, and I was awed by the layout of the city and the beautiful walking trails and the respect shown for the statues and the monuments. These monuments take years of planning. They are not thrown up on the whim of one man. They are planned carefully, money raised and then constructed with all the due respect that they deserve. I am almost 70 years old. I have watched our country change over time. Some great things have happened but many, many awful things have, too. We cannot allow this arch to be built.

name: Tracy Ballesteros
text: strongly encourage the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) to vote no on the proposed Monumental Arch. The open space between Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and the Lincoln Memorial was intentionally designed to provide a solemn, respectful, and unobstructed view shed befitting one of our nation's most sacred commemorative landscapes. This space was never intended to be developed or visually dominated by a new monumental structure. The Memorial Circle serves an important civic and symbolic purpose and should remain open and undeveloped. Introducing a large memorial arch into this setting would fundamentally alter the historic character and visual integrity of the landscape, diminishing the dignity and contemplative nature of the area. Once this precedent is set, the integrity of this nationally significant memorial corridor becomes increasingly vulnerable to future encroachment. In addition to concerns about historical intent and preservation, the proposal raises serious questions regarding public safety and infrastructure impacts. Under ordinary planning and compliance practices, a comprehensive traffic and visitor impact study would be essential. The location already experiences heavy vehicular, pedestrian, bicycle, and ceremonial traffic. Adding a major tourist destination at this highly constrained intersection creates foreseeable safety and congestion concerns that should not be minimized. The plan to construct a memorial arch in this location is fundamentally inconsistent with the intended purpose, historic character, and respectful solemnity of this landscape. I respectfully urge the NCPC to reject this proposal and vote no.

name: Ellen Bromfield
text: I oppose the building of the proposed Monumental Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway, near Arlington National Cemetery and along the Potomac River. The location of the proposed Arch will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. It is because this viewshed carries so much meaning to the country that the National Trust has raised concerns about the proposed Monumental Arch, whose scale, location, and design will disrupt this important visual and symbolic vista. The Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. name: Elizabeth Rummage
text: A Statement in Opposition to the Proposed Triumphal Arch of Washington, D.C. The proposed Triumphal Arch, a 250-foot granite structure topped with a 24-carat gold-plated statue and modeled after the Arc de Triomphe in Paris represents a profound misjudgment on multiple fronts: aesthetic, practical, and fiscal. As a citizen who holds the integrity of our national capital in the highest regard, I urge the National Capital Planning Commission and all relevant authorities to reject this project outright. A Violation of Washington's Visual Identity Washington, D.C. was designed with deliberate restraint and harmony. Its skyline, sightlines, and monumental core reflect a careful civic vision accumulated over centuries. At 250 feet tall, this arch would be taller than any other arch in any national capital, and urban planning experts have already noted it would be "way too big for that site." The proposed location near Arlington Memorial Bridge would place an overwhelming foreign-style monument in direct competition with the quiet dignity of Arlington National Cemetery and the existing memorial landscape. A group of Vietnam War veterans has already filed suit, arguing the structure would obscure views of other monuments from the cemetery. Airspace and Safety Concerns The arch's height would make it the second-tallest structure in the D.C. skyline, second only to the Washington Monument. In a city with some of the most tightly managed and sensitive airspace in the world, home to Reagan National Airport, restricted government flight corridors, and military operations, introducing a towering new structure of this scale demands serious scrutiny that has not been adequately provided. Fiscal Recklessness in an Era of Insolvency Perhaps most damning is the financial picture. The White House has not provided a cost estimate for the project, an astonishing omission for a structure of this ambition and scale. At a time when the federal government carries historic debt and citizens are being asked to absorb cuts to essential services, the administration proposes an architectural vanity project with no price tag and no accountability. That funding mechanisms and long-term maintenance costs remain subjects of debate is not a minor procedural footnote but a fundamental failure of governance. A Voice Ignored Most tellingly, the people have already spoken. During a May 2026 public hearing, commissioners were told that 99.5 percent of over 600 public comments opposed the structure. The commission approved it anyway. When the body charged with representing the public interest dismisses near-unanimous opposition from the public, something has gone deeply wrong. It bears noting that in October 2025, Trump took the unusual step of firing six sitting members of the commission, replacing them entirely with his own appointees; making the approval process little more than a formality. History is watching. Great civilizations are remembered not only for what they built, but for the wisdom they showed in knowing what not to build — and why. This arch is a monument to neither liberty nor justice. It is a monument to unchecked ambition at public expense. It must be stopped.

name: Robin Tryloff
text: To the Members of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts: I respectfully submit the following comments regarding the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. I strongly oppose the proposal as currently designed and urge the Commission to withhold approval pending completion of the Section 106 review process and substantial reconsideration of the project's location, scale, and visual impact. The proposed Arch would fundamentally disrupt one of the most meaningful symbolic landscapes in the United States: the axial relationship connecting the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. This carefully designed vista represents national reconciliation following the Civil War and has long been protected through thoughtful planning decisions that preserve open views and visual harmony across the monumental core of Washington. The proposed structure would severely compromise that historic composition. Its massive scale and vertical prominence would interrupt the intentional sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House and overwhelm the restrained profile of Arlington Memorial Bridge, which was specifically designed to preserve these symbolic relationships. I am also deeply concerned about the extraordinary height and monumentality of the proposal. A structure of this scale—particularly with the large sculptural element proposed atop the Arch—would dominate surrounding historic resources, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Rather than complementing the existing commemorative landscape, it would compete with and diminish it. The National Mall and its associated memorial landscapes are successful because they maintain a clear hierarchy of monumental spaces and preserve long, open viewsheds. The proposed Arch is inconsistent with this historic planning framework, including the principles established by the McMillan Plan that have guided stewardship of the monumental core for more than a century. The proposal is especially inappropriate at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery. Arlington is not merely a ceremonial setting; it is an active and solemn national cemetery where military families continue to bury loved ones every day. Its power derives from dignity, restraint, uniformity, and reverence. A monumental triumphal structure of this size and character risks undermining the contemplative and sacred atmosphere that defines Arlington National Cemetery. Finally, I urge the Commission to defer action until the legally required Section 106 review process under the National Historic Preservation Act has been completed. That consultation process exists precisely to evaluate impacts on historic and cultural resources and to ensure informed public participation before approval decisions are made. Proceeding prior to completion of that process would be premature. Thank you for your consideration of these comments and for your continued stewardship of the Nation's historic commemorative landscape.

text: I am writing as a concerned American citizen to urge the National Capital Planning Commission to reject the proposed 250-foot triumphal arch at Memorial Circle. This project is wrong on multiple levels, and I believe the Commission has both the authority and the obligation to say so. It disrespects our veterans. The proposed site sits at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery which is hallowed ground where hundreds of thousands of Americans who gave their lives in service to this country are buried. Placing a gaudy, gilded monument to a living president at the threshold of that sacred space is an insult to their sacrifice and to the families who visit them. A triumphal arch is a celebration. Arlington is a place of reverence. These are incompatible. It would permanently damage an irreplaceable viewshed. The visual corridor between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery is one of the most historically significant sightlines in the United States. At more than twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial, this structure would dominate and forever alter that landscape. Washington's monumental core was deliberately designed. This project would vandalise it. It sets a dangerous precedent. Our tradition has always been to memorialize presidents and public figures after history has had time to render a verdict. Building a monument to a sitting president — one explicitly compared by its proponents to the Arc de Triumph abandons that principle entirely. The monument's purpose is self-glorification, not public commemoration. The costs are unaccounted for. No final cost estimate exists. The administration has floated a vague mix of taxpayer and private money, with no transparency about how much of the public's money will be spent. At a time of significant fiscal pressure on ordinary Americans, this is not an appropriate use of federal resources. I urge the Commission to vote no. Future generations will inherit whatever we build here. They deserve better than this.

name: Lori Johnson
text: I visited Washington DC this spring with my grandson. Seeing the Lincoln Memorial was the highlight of his trip. The proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House.

name: Dinah Zeltser
text: Dear NCPC I fully concur with the comments below submitted by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. As a resident of DC and frequent visitor to the area under consideration for construction I urgently urge you to respect the wishes of DC residents to not build an Arch. The National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States ("National Trust") is a private charitable, educational, nonprofit corporation headquartered in Washington, D.C. and chartered by Congress in 1949 to further the historic preservation policy of the United States. 54 U.S.C. § 312102(a). This Congressional charter obligates the National Trust to "facilitate public participation in the preservation of sites, buildings, and objects of national significance or interest." We respectfully submit the following comments concerning the current proposal by the Executive Office of the President and the U.S. Department of the Interior to construct a new Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. We urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do "not interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work," and "to the maximum extent practicable, it protects open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." 40 U.S.C. § 8905(b)(2). We would also remind the Commissioners that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. Id. § 8903. After reviewing the revised concept plans that have been submitted to CFA, the National Trust remains concerned about the location, height, scale, and design of the proposed Triumphal Arch, the manner in which it interferes with existing commemorative works and fails to protect existing public uses and cultural resources. Notwithstanding comments and recommendations by Commission members at the April 2026 meeting, the modifications to the proposal have been minimal. Most notably, the 68-foot-high sculpture at the top of the proposed Arch has not been removed or reduced, contrary to the Commissioners' recommendation. In addition, the revised proposal does not appear to include secondary open archways within the legs of the central arch in order to make it more open, as recommended by the Commissioners. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. The National Trust is also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission's own staff. We urge the Commission members to defer any decision in order to be informed by the Section 106 process.

name: Sheryl Bower
text: I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed commemorative arch. This proposal is fundamentally out of context with the historic planning framework of Washington, DC, and it raises significant concerns about process, precedent, and responsible stewardship of public resources. The arch conflicts with the L'Enfant and McMillan Plans, which form the backbone of the city's nationally protected urban design. These plans emphasize open vistas, axial clarity, and a cohesive neoclassical vocabulary. Introducing a monumental structure of this nature — without integration into the established planning language — would undermine the historical integrity that the NCPC is charged with preserving. Equally troubling is the lack of transparent vetting. Major additions to the monumental core require rigorous review, public consultation, and expert evaluation. This proposal has not undergone the standard design competition, stakeholder engagement, or feasibility analysis expected for projects of this scale. Advancing it without those steps would set a damaging precedent for bypassing established federal planning processes. The project also represents a misuse of taxpayer funds. At a time when federal agencies face competing infrastructure, maintenance, and public‐service needs, allocating substantial resources to a discretionary commemorative structure is neither fiscally responsible nor aligned with broader public priorities. Finally, the proposal reads as a self‐referential monument, rather than a contribution to the shared civic landscape. Washington's monumental core is reserved for symbols of national significance, not personal commemoration. Allowing an unvetted, individual‐focused structure would erode the principles that have guided federal planning for more than a century. For these reasons, I urge the NCPC to reject the proposed arch and reaffirm its commitment to historically grounded, publicly accountable, and fiscally responsible planning for the nation's capital.

name: Martin Rose
text: PUBLIC COMMENT DRAFT (Legal‐Hook Version) Subject: Comment on Proposed Monumental Arch – Procedural and Statutory Concerns I submit this comment to request that the National Capital Planning Commission refrain from advancing the proposed monumental arch until the project complies with all statutory requirements under the Commemorative Works Act (CWA), the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). 1. Commemorative Works Act (CWA) Applicability The proposed arch appears to constitute a "commemorative work" under 40 U.S.C. § 8902(a). If so, the project requires explicit congressional authorization. I request that NCPC clarify: • Whether the project has been formally classified as a commemorative work • Whether congressional authorization has been obtained • Whether the proposed site lies within Area I or Area II • Whether the project complies with the statutory prohibition on new commemorative works on the National Mall If the project is being treated as non‐commemorative, I request disclosure of the legal rationale for that determination, including any written opinions or internal guidance. 2. NEPA Compliance and Alternatives Analysis A monumental structure of this scale constitutes a major federal action requiring a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). I request that NCPC ensure: • A full range of reasonable alternatives is evaluated, including the "no‐build" alternative • Visual, cultural, and transportation impacts are analyzed • Cumulative impacts are addressed • Public scoping meetings are held prior to any decision Any attempt to rely on a Categorical Exclusion or abbreviated Environmental Assessment would be inconsistent with NEPA case law for projects of this magnitude. 3. Section 106 Consultation Requirements The proposed arch would affect multiple historic resources, including the L'Enfant Plan, the McMillan Plan, and adjacent historic districts. I request confirmation that: • Consulting parties have been invited • Tribal consultation has been initiated • Area of Potential Effects (APE) has been defined • Alternatives and mitigation measures will be developed through the Section 106 process 4. Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) Jurisdiction Because the project is monumental in scale and symbolic in character, CFA review is required under the CWA and the Shipstead‐Luce Act. • I request that NCPC clarify the sequencing of CFA review and whether CFA has been consulted regarding the conceptual design. 5. Request for Transparency and Documentation To ensure a legally adequate administrative record, I request that NCPC make publicly available: • All classification memos regarding CWA applicability • Any correspondence with congressional committees • Any preliminary NEPA documentation • Any Section 106 initiation letters • Any interagency design review comments Conclusion Until the project complies with the CWA, NEPA, and NHPA, NCPC should not advance it beyond preliminary review. Failure to follow these statutory requirements would expose the project to significant legal vulnerability under the Administrative Procedure Act. Thank you for considering these comments. Martin. A. Rose
