name: Rita Beyers
text: To th National Capital Planning Commission: I concur with the following statements, previously submitted by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, regarding the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. I am strongly opposed to the construction of the arch for the reasons listed below. In addition, our tax dollars could be put to much better use and this project has not been approved, as required by law, by the U.S. Congress. The National Trust's comments follow: "We respectfully submit the following comments concerning the current proposal by the Executive Office of the President and the U.S. Department of the Interior to construct a new Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. We urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." We would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. After reviewing the revised concept plans that have been submitted to CFA, the National Trust remains concerned about the location, height, scale, and design of the proposed Triumphal Arch, the manner in which it interferes with existing commemorative works and fails to protect existing public uses and cultural resources. Notwithstanding comments and recommendations by Commission members at the April 2026 meeting, the modifications to the proposal have been minimal. Most notably, the 68-foot-high sculpture at the top of the proposed Arch has not been removed or reduced, contrary to the Commissioners' recommendation. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. The National Trust is also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission itself. We urge the Commission members to await the Section 106 process, which has not yet been initiated." It is my understanding that comments regarding this proposed arch have been overwhelmingly against its construction. I would hope that the Commission would take seriously the negative reaction to the proposed arch and reject the proposal. Thank you.

The American people do not want this arch, we do not want our tax dollars to go to this thing, on this 250th anniversary we should be celebrating the diversity that made this country, not the hate that this arch represents.

name: Peggy Asplund
text: I oppose the construction of the monumental arch until a legitimate, lawful review is conducted. The destruction of the White House without going through proper review is a criminal act. The construction of this monstrosity should at least go through proper review where any sane person could see that this arch and its location is a disruption to the original views uniting Lee's house and the cemetery to the Lincoln Memorial. This historic view should be preserved. Additionally the proposed arch would obliterate the view of JFK's eternal flame. Thank you for considering my comments which I believe speak for the majority of US citizens.

name: Suzanne Delp
text: I submit my strong disapproval and anger at the building of this monument. In my opinion it will be an eyesore and an expense that.has no legitimate basis. This money should be spent on the American people.

name: Ernie deVried
text: I object to the construction a a memorial arch at this location. This would be a desecration of holy ground that speaks so loudly of our nation's history. The proposed arch is too large, and is gaudy, as well as being clearly intended to "honor" a president who does not understand the meaning of that term. But my objection is not personal. The symbolism of Arlington, the Lincoln Memorial, and the Washington Monument and their relationship to each other is important. Constructing this arch is a blasphemy, regardless of who builds it.

name: Cara Sargent
text: No. Absolutely not. Thos is a ridiculous proposal. The thing would be torn down pretty soon, anyway.

name: Thomas Best
text: The proposed arch, which is opposed by the vast majority of the American people and various veteran groups, is going to inhibit the stunning views of both Arlington National Cemetery but the Lincoln Memorial as well. Our nation's capital is not a place for a so-called "Triumphant Arch" which appears more to glorify Donald Trump than celebrate any achievement of the American people. Mark me as a solid no.

name: Annette Dluger
text: I am totally opposed to building an arch which interferes with the views toward Arlington national Cemetery. It is disrespectful to veterans and a hazard to air traffic. In fact, such an arch has no place in the District of Columbia. The money could be better spent in providing funds for research to the NIH.

name: Michele Resue
text: Pretty easy... NO ARCH !!!!

name: Ellen Mallory
text: I strongly oppose the proposed new monumental arch. Its location would destroy the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. This one of the most symbolic landscapes in Washington, D.C.. The vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. The proposed arch's scale, location, and design will disrupt this important visual and symbolic vista that has so much meaning for our country. As well, it will overwhelm the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity.

name: Nicole Bendick
text: France already has an arch. We don't need to copy. The direct line of sight from Lincoln memorial to Arlington should not be tampered with. It's already a breathtaking sight and we shouldn't mess with it. The proposed arch looks tacky and messes with a historical connection that shouldn't be interfered with.

name: Melissa Monti
text: I urgently request that you disallow the planned large arch near the Arlington Bridge. The enormous size and position will obscure the historically important view between Arlington Cemetery, Arlington House and the Lincoln Memorial. Our Capital City was carefully designed to provide focus on historic sights and I am totally opposed to changes driven by one person. His ideas should not take precedence above those from the National Trust for Historic Preservation and citizens like me.

name: Kristine Enright
text: I am wholeheartedly against a Monumental Arch. President Trump has already destroyed enough at the White House and does not need to do any more damage to our historic spaces!

name: Renee Sessler
text: I agree wholeheartedly with the following and go on the record as an American that I oppose the proposed arch. I urge the commission to not approve. " The location of the proposed Arch will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscapes in Washington, D.C., the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. It is because this viewshed carries so much meaning to the country that the National Trust has raised concerns about the proposed Monumental Arch, whose scale, location, and design will disrupt this important visual and symbolic vista. In addition, the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital."

name: Marcia Spear
text: I strenuously object to the building of Trump's arch. Our presidents should not be building monuments to their own ego. It is ugly and does not fit with the other correct monuments and cemetery in that area. The pictures and names on buildings need to go. It is a disgrace and cheapens our capitol city. Nix the ballroom and the militarization of the White House, rebuild the East Wing at his expense, restore the Kennedy Center, and ditch the gold in the White House. These things belong to the American people, not a part-time squatter with no class.

name: Miranda Zywicki
text: I am against the arch as it is a waste of taxpayer money. The funds for the New Monumental Arch should instead go to a project in which President Donald J. Trump can support the American people. A copy-cat of a project from St. Louis is not the answer, supporting the entry of countries like Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, and other Arab countries to the Abraham Accords, created by President Donald J. Trump, is the way to go. I support our President, Mr. Donald J. Trump, in creating a legacy for himself by making America great; President Donald J. Trump can do this through his own plan: the Abraham Accords.

name: Christine Tomasik
text: Dear Esteemed Members of the National Capital Planning Commission, I would like to express my sincere concerns about the proposed New Monumental Arch. The Commemorative Works Act states that new projects should not interfere with existing commemorative works. From my understanding of this project, in its proposed dimensions, the arch would interfere with the existing commemorative works of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. I would urge the NCPC and the National Park Service, under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, to participate in a thorough review and consider alternatives to the design and location of the arch. In this process, the project re-design would then be brought before Congress for their approval, as required by the Commemorative Works Act. So many loved ones are buried in Arlington National Cemetery; my dear friend's husband, my high school classmate's father, and another dear friend's parents. I would feel personally distraught if this arch, as proposed, moved forward; I can only imagine how they would feel. The location, height, and scale would interfere with the visual landscape now enjoyed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Moving forward with this project would disrespect all of the veterans buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Sincerely, Christine

name: Denise Hall
text: I am writing in opposition to the monumental arch. There are many reasons I am against it. First it interferes with the intended relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetary. It is an inappropriate entrance to the National Cemetary. It's size also hides the view of other monuments. It is unnecessary and will destroy this revered area of our nation.

name: Judy Stokesberry
text: Please accept my strong objections to a monumental arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. This is not a monument to our nation, but to the ego of one man. Instead of a monumental arch, I suggest a memorial to teachers who spend their entire lives working at low wages to improve the lives of our children.

name: Margaret Summers
text: I am writing in opposition to the New Monumental Arch project. There are multiple reasons this project is not feasible, including the cost, the traffic, and the purpose. The cost of this project, we can be sure, would be an irresponsible amount to spend. Traffic during construction, and after completion, would cause huge problems for all. Finally, the purpose of this is clearly a vanity project that I fully oppose. Please do not build this.

name: Diane Tracy
text: I am against the construction of the Monumental Arch as it will destroy the historical view and overpower the surrounding features and views of the present day monuments and National Cemetery. Also it resembles Military and Nazi symbolisms with the large golden eagles.

name: Kelly O'Connor
text: NO UGLY ARCH for the TRUMP REGIME

name: Julie Chapman
text: I cannot begin to understand why ANYONE would countenance the construction of this monstrosity. This is appalling, disgusting, and vomitous. We can call it L'Arc de Treason, given the many ways Trump has undermined our nation's laws and the Constitution, tossed away our allies, trampled our economy, tried to steal top-secret files -- including his repulsive proposal to steal money from taxpayers to give to insurrectionists. Or perhaps L'Arc d'Epstein-Trump files. STOP THIS!!

name: Janice MacKenzie
text: This arch is not at all appropriate in scale or design as it would dominate the approach to Arlington Cemetery. In addition, it is not in keeping with the historic theme and respectful timing of the installation of monuments that honor our past heroes who "gave their last full measure of devotion". It is rushed and has been given little thought other than in its size. This arch is a vainglorious attempt to dominate the surrounding structures or the bridge, and in no way respects the site or the sacrifice of past patriots buried at Arlington.

name: William Brower
text: It is an abomination and totally un-American. We do NOT build monuments to living politicians!

name: Nancy Weil
text: This piece, designed to honor one man, must be stopped. It is not in keeping with the area's current design and is nothing more than a waste of tax dollars.

name: Elizabeth Lockwood
text: I am opposed to my tax dollars being spent for the creation of a new monumental arch. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. The project is offensive to the carefully laid out plans to commemorate important events in American history, and disrespectful of those in Arlington cemetery who gave their lives for this country. Please do not approve this project.

name: Kathy Preston
text: I am against the use of tax payer dollars to fund the monumental arch when we are a country at war and prices are soaring. Our country is in such financial debt that future generations will struggle to repay or ever recover from the reckless spending of this administration. This is a vanity project the people do not support. I'm so disappointed in you.

name: Karen Leverich
text: Hello, I am greatly disturbed to hear about the possible arch being built in Washington DC. I am a retired school teacher. After retiring from teaching, I became a tour director for such companies as Globus, Smithsonian, Destination America. I spent several months studying the city of Washington, so that I could take the exam and become a qualified tour guide of the city. What I and my passengers were most impressed about when visiting Washington, was the historical significance of the architecture and the history they represented. It is a shame what this administration has done to the White House. Please not another eyesore in the form of an Arch.

name: Barbara Weber
text: The proposed Monumental Arch should not be approved. The scale, style and location are inconsistent with - and damaging to - the important and meaningful viewsheds of our nation's capital. The proposal lacks care for, and insight into, the significance and symbolism of the nearby national monuments and Arlington Cemetery. The idea of the Monumental Arch is rushed and, although it will dominate other monuments in size, it is dwarfed in meaning and significance by the surrounding monuments. The creation of the Monumental Arch at the proposed location would be a tragic mistake.

name: Richard Morrison
text: Good day; I would like to express my objection to the proposed arch. The size and scale of this project will dwarf almost all other monuments in the city. As the entry to Arlington cemetery, it will change the design that had painstaking done earlier. Please keep the Capital free from quick political designs. Sincerely, Richard Morrison Dallas, TX

name: Susan Brothers
text: Stop this ego project that will block the historic planned view of Arlington Cemetery. Tacky, overly huge and embarrassing. Please don't allow yet another vanity project to blight our history. The solemn nature of Arlington is not a carnival show. Everything he touches is blighted by a sex offender and felon who is raping the country daily. STOP THE DISRESPECTFUL ARCH.

name: Tamara Purdum
text: Until every veteran who fought for this country is NO LONGER homeless or lacking good health support DO NOT BUILD THIS TRUMP ARCH

name: Catharine Kristian
text: Any new memorial or functional structure to the National Mall or any other federal space needs a full design, structural, and esoteric evaluation on the structure proposed. It also must be evaluated on the historical significance of the structure to our country's history. Our nation has relied on our government bodies, including legislative and executive branches, to thoroughly evaluate any structure that would take a significant position on federal land. We must continue this practice and not rush into any decision proposed by any member of Congress, the Judicial or Executive branch of the U.S. government.

name: Stephen Gronek
text: NO ARCH. No meaning only a vanity project!

name: Jacqueline Solomon
text: Dear Commissioners- I oppose the proposed "New Monumental Arch." The lack of a formal design process, lack of consideration of alternative locations, lack of thoughtful selection of a qualified artist and lack of attention to detail/scale/aesthetic that I believe most Americans would assume and expect to occur when adding anything permanent to the National Mall in our nation's capital city is unconscionable. Being mindful of the important symbolic and historic connections between the Mall and Arlington Cemetery is something that takes time and must be done in a thoughtful manner that listens to all concerns and respects the existing built environment. This oversized and as proposed, in my opinion, VERY GAUDY and VERY UGLY arch will detract from the historic beauty and majesty of our nation's capital. Please return this application to the proposing parties and make them follow a more formal process that includes input from people, organizations and subject experts from all over the United States to ensure that, if eventually approved, an arch fits in with tone and scale of the original plans for our capital and is designed to incorporate elements of our diverse nation in the details and proposed scenes on the arch. The Vietnam Memorial Wall is an excellent example of how a new element was successfully added to the area and provides a profound emotional experience and appropriately honors those killed in that war. The Vietnam Memorial Wall was required to follow more formal design and approval process than it appears is being contemplated for this New Monumental Arch. This commission's input should be an important part of a larger public approval process. The National Park Service staff and budget should be reserved for projects that have been contemplated and included in their Capital Improvement Plans. Our country and our National Parks Service staff deserve better than to be rushed into a new project, when they already had a large number of projects to implement and complete to keep our amazing National Park System functional, updated and accessible to all. As a nod to our country's 250th anniversary, if this "New Monumental Arch" was eventually constructed as currently proposed, it would only serve to remind of me and many of my fellow citizens of this extremely disturbing and upsetting time in our country's history. I don't think that is what the applicant is hoping for in the long or short term. Thank you for your consideration. Jacqueline Solomon Danville, California

name: Elizabeth Starrs
text: Please, please hear our pleas! We do not want that monstrous arch! We especially don't want to pay for it either! We know the President likes to say that his pet projects will be " privately funded" but we can see this doesn't actually happen! JUST SAY NO !

name: Chris Gralapp
text: Dear NCPC, thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed Arch. Given the state of the economy for average Americans, I feel that the budgeted expenditures for this project could be much better directed toward finding solutions for the affordability crisis. The administration is clearly tone deaf to the plight of ordinary citizens, and all of these gaudy, meaningless monuments to a single person are not sitting well with the majority of the people of our great country. What would the founders feel about these empty, unpatriotic projects? And while you are at it, please put a halt to the Ballroom! So blatantly wrong, in so many ways, and a desecration of democracy. Please decline to authorize this boondoggle of a 'monument'. Chris Gralapp

name: Mary Doherty
text: As you stated so well the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. My husband was an Army Medic stationed in Korea during the Vietnam War. He is buried in a military cemetery. I am deeply offended by the lack of respect and honor the proposed arch shows towards all of our veterans. Thank you for the chance to object to the construction of this arch.

name: Diana Blankenship
text: I feel the proposal would detract from the dignity and current landscape of the Lincoln memorial and Washington memorial. There is no purpose for this project other than stroking the ego of the man in the presidency, who is a convicted felon.

name: Elaine Treado
text: I cannot believe the destruction of my hometown, historic Washington, D.C. I do not understand how this president has gotten away with tearing down part of the White House and starting a building project that would usually take years to get approval for. And now, this arch. An abomination. I had more trouble getting approval for a pool built in my backyard than trump has had in defacing our Nation's capital. I do not understand how any of this has not been stopped.

name: Deborah Hecker
text: Please, please, please do whatever is possible to prevent the erection of the proposed monumental arch. So much has been destroyed or atrociously altered recently in our nation's capital. We do not need another costly monstrosity.

name: Jennifer Cuddeback
text: It is imperative this NOT be constructed. There is no need for it, it represents nothing, and it a complete waste of money.

name: Kathie Gordon-Brooks
text: I do not support building a monumental arch in Washington DC. I believe the existing monuments must be maintained and that they provide the proper way to honor our history. The monumental arch is ugly, grotesque and meant to honor one person, not history. Please deny this project.

name: Louise Beer
text: As a concerned citizen, I oppose the monumental arch based on the following: * Disrupted Historic Views: The proposed site—a roundabout between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery—is a protected view shed created to symbolize reunification after the Civil War. Critics, historians, and veterans argue that a 250-foot structure would dominate and destroy this iconic vista. * Lack of Congressional Authorization: New commemorations and major construction on federal parkland in the capital require Congressional approval. * Extreme Scale: At 250 feet, the arch is nearly twice the height allowed by the federal Height of Buildings Act. It is more than twice as tall as the Lincoln Memorial and close to half the height of the Washington Monument. * Safety & Traffic Concerns: Because the location sits in a busy traffic roundabout near the flight path of Reagan National Airport, pedestrian safety and aviation-clearance are at risk.

name: Jennifer Estep
text: Please do not erect a hideous arch that is out of scale with the carefully planned surroundings. We are America, and we have our own original monuments - we don't have to copy the triumphal arches of other countries like Hitler wanted to do.

name: Jonathan Kelsey
text: The location of the proposed Arch will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscapes in Washington, D.C., the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. It is because this viewshed carries so much meaning to the country that the National Trust has raised concerns about the proposed Monumental Arch, whose scale, location, and design will disrupt this important visual and symbolic vista. In addition, the Arch will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, overwhelming the entry to Arlington National Cemetery—the hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families and a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of our Capitol.

name: Sheryl Harris
text: Dear NCPC, I am writing to oppose the proposed monumental arch at Washington DC. I do not believe this project reflects the priorities or character of our country. The cost, size, and overall negative impact on existing monuments raise concerns, and with the national debt soaring resources could be better used elsewhere. I respectfully ask that the proposal be rejected. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Sheryl Harris

name: Diana Merrifield
text: Dear Commission, I was a resident of Washington DC and Alexandria Virginia for 25 years. I whole heartedly object to this arch on so many principles. As the daughter and granddaughter of veterans who gave their lives to this country, this proposed arch defiles their memory and the solemnity of the expanse between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National cemetery. I would argue we already have memorial arches in the Memorial Bridge. Our Capitol city is beautiful and the thought of a monstrous arch makes me weep for the soul of our country. It doesn't reflect the best of us, but imperial instincts best left to history. Please use restraint and maintain the current contemplative green spaces from which we honor those who gave all. Please. A nation begs you to do the right thing.

name: Karen Buys
text: I am writing to voice my strong objection to the proposed monumental arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Leaving aside for the moment the tasteless design of the arch and its oversized statue, my deepest concern is for the disrespect that it shows to our honored dead by interrupting the vista linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. It is shameful that any president, much less one who has performed no military service, would presume to memorialize himself at the expense of those who fought and died for our nation. It is still worse that this president proposes to do so by aping the imperialist, authoritarian triumphal arches of corrupt Roman emperors and the fascist regimes they inspired. "Architecture is a language; it has something to say. What this monument wants to say is that the ego of one man is worth the desecration of the memory of thousands of others. In doing so, it dishonors those dead and the country for which they fought. Its construction should not be permitted."

name: Elaine Senft
text: This would be a terrible waste of money to begin with. Moreover, it would ruin the views between several of the existing monuments and memorials and degrade the importance of those monuments and memorials.

name: Sharon Heim
text: I object to the construction of a massive arch that will permanently alter the historic planned view shed that already exists. This is a narsacistic project by a narsacistic man to glorify only himself for the corruption and treasonous actions he is carrying out. There has been no Section 106 evaluation. There has been no consideration of alternative locations. There has only been the demands made by a delusional man determined to destroy not just the country he is supposed to be leading, but the very history of the country to appease his pathetic ego. This project should not be allowed to move forward and if it does, it will need to be removed and the area and the historic line of sight be restored.

name: Carole Shrader
text: It's a ridiculous monstrosity and a huge waste of money.

name: Julie Berg
text: The concept of this arch is lost on me as a United States citizen. It overshadows one of the greatest memorials we have in Arlington National Cemetery. We know what that site represents! it is a place of honor and a show of respect for those who made the ultimate sacrifice for our country. The design of this proposed arch is gaudy in size and materials. What is the point? Please, no arch!!!!

name: Gayle Vuletic
text: I think that our money needs to be spent elsewhere. I think the way Arlington looks now, is fine. If you go to the American Cemetery in Normandy, there is no arch there. It is peaceful. That is how Arlington should be, peaceful and without ornamentation.

name: Catherine Arwood Hall
text: This extravagant proposed monument would interrupt the view of already established memorials and is extremely unnecessary!

name: Ellen Sollod
text: Oppose the so-called new monumental arch. This is a travesty and a violation of the historical integrity of the site. This enormous eyesore will dwarf Arlington National Cemetery and desecrate the solemnness of this site. It will undermine the relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and the original origins of the Cemetery. It is an affront to patriots who hold the historical importance of the Capitol monuments dear. I am utterly appalled by the kutzpah of Trump to blatantly propose this ugly eyesore for this important site. It is equally appalling that people who have been appointed to this commission have such blatant disregard for historic preservation and design integrity. Approving this undermines any credibility that they would hope to have.

name: Mike Hunt
text: For many years, the United States of America worked Ceaselessly to promote the welfare of our Kin and kindred spirits home and abroad. Today, I must Respectfully recommend against this Undertaking as it is a waste of Money, is tone deaf during a war, and lacks a Purpose that such resources demand.

name: Robby Marvin
text: I'm concerned that the project related to the New Monument Arch has not gone through the appropriate levels of review. Please consider what this large monumwnt does to interfere with the current historic landscape. I'm not opposed to building such monuments. There may be other more suitable locations for said monument that donnot interfere with the historic scene that the monument is currently being proposed.

name: Malinda Brown
text: From the description of the way this arch will change the carefully planned view of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery, I ask that this project be abandoned, or at the very least, studied much more in depth.

name: LESLIE MATTESON
text: There are too many veterans that do not want to see this arch. It is too big and ugly, to destroys the views and landscape. These things should be designed be a group that works together to include ALL of America.

name: Maureen Chapman
text: I am strongly opposed to this proposed project, its size, cost and complete absence of any rationale for building it, particularly in the proposed location. It is a travesty and will dishonor the legacy of all who served the U.S., many of whom died in service to this country, and are buried in Arlington Cemetery. Please stop this project from being built.

name: Donna Sparber
text: This arch will destroy the solemn view of Arlington National Cemetery and dishonor the patriots who rest there. Cancel this project.

name: Ruth Karavanic
text: I vehemently object to Trump's latest vanity project. Arlington is sacred ground and needs to be solemnly left alone. This man was not elected to rebuild Washington, DC to his liking. Enough with the vanity projects. He needs to stick to his job description for President of the United States. It is time to tell this man NO and to go back to his Oval Office and work on real problems like getting us out of Uran's business, stabilizing our economy and reducing the deficit. It's time he started working on his concept of a plan, fulfilling his campaign promises and getting ICE, Patel and Hegseth in order. PLEASE, someone have the guts to tell him no.

name: Heath Lynn Silberfeld
text: Regarding the proposed monumental arch, there are numerous reasons why construction should not proceed, at least at this time. First, established procedures for design and review have not been followed. Second, the president alone has not been given the authority to decide about this on his own. Third, we are a young country and changes to our established ways of moving things through an approval process should be followed in order for THE PEOPLE to have a say in the outcome of proposed changes. Fourth, the destruction of the East Wing and the current work at the Reflecting Pool without authority are indicative of the careless and thoughtless way that the president goes about making changes that result in messes and costly overruns, if not outright grifting. I could go on, but I trust that these reasons are sufficient to support you in insisting that normal review processes and procedures be followed in this and any future changes to the landscape of our precious Capitol: Washington, District of Columbia. Thank you for your attention to this matter! HLS

name: Jackson Helms
text: I do not support the proposed arch. The proposed arch lacks function, aesthetic appeal, and fiscal sense.

name: Margaret Miller
text: HELL,no. No monument to one of the most corrupt, evil, heartless, anti-democratic presidents in our history. The monument is bloated and oversized and awkward in its placement much like he is. I beg you not to let this happen.

name: Janet Stoegerer
text: I object to the arch being built that will obstruct the view from Arlington Cemetery where my mother-in-law and her husband are buried. I object to any reminder of the current President who has shown disdain for fallen patriots.

name: Linda Krause
text: I would respectfully like to submit my objection to the Monumental Arch that is being proposed. We do not need an arch for a President first of all, and especially one that will tower over our other great monuments that commemorate great Presidents. The cost also is prohibitive. Our Country cannot afford this frivolous expense. I thanks you very much for your consideration. Sincerely, Linda Krause

name: David Frankel
text: I've been living in Washington DC since 1980 — 46 years. I strongly oppose the construction of an arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. An arch will block the view of the memorial from Arlington Cemetery. I urge you to reject this proposal. David P. Frankel Washington DC

name: Jill Heryford
text: Please no. Considering sight lines being blocked for this monstrosity. No. No.

name: Pamela Sherrod
text: This proposed project is a desecration of our nation's capital and should be roundly rejected.

name: JeVerna Haynes
text: Under NO circumstances do I want to see or pay for a monumental arch to ruin the historial layout of the cemetery to the Lincoln Memorial. Donald Trump knows nothing of our history. I do. He has already ruined the White House and the reflecting pool where I spent more hours than I could even count. Damn that bastard! He is trying to build monuments to himself when all he should ever be entitled to is maybe, maybe, a tombstone. NO NO NO!

name: Patty More
text: I oppose the incredibly disrespectful building of the arch. The current president is hell bent on plastering homages to himself on every piece of land and property without regard to we the people's wishes.

name: Peg Herring
text: I do not want the arch. We don't need it. It will disrupt the landscape. It will take funds away from necessary projects. It is a vanity project for the President.

name: Christina Fullerton
text: Please, please put this somewhere else or better yet, don't build it at all. We have such symbolism and purity in the aesthetics of our capital. Don't ruin it.

name: Dianne Ham
text: This is a waste of tax-payer dollars, a monumental vanity project that should not be permitted for what it is, and an eyesore on our capitol.

name: Helen Shafton
text: Please protect this beautiful view of this sacred American place from desecration. Ask veterans and families of the fallen what they think. One man, who temporarily resides in the White House, should not be allowed to leave such an enormous and lasting blemish on our nation's capital!

name: Judy Greenblum
text: I do not support a monumental arch at Memorial Circle and am strongly against it. I am the widow of a U.S. Marine veteran who is buried at Arlington Cemetery. Residing only 15 minutes away, I visit the Cemetery several times a year and drive around Memorial Circle on each visit. On a practical level, it is challenging enough to navigate the Circle safely. Building a monument in the center would impede visibility and distract drivers. On a personal level and more importantly, the Arch would detract from the solemnity of each visit to Arlington Cemetery. The approach along Memorial Drive would be interrupted and reduce the focus on Arlington Cemetery and honoring our country's military service members, veterans and prominent public figures. The view of the Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument from Memorial Drive leaving Arlington Cemetery (and, especially, from Arlington House) is breathtaking. This would be lost by erecting the Arch. We do not need a grandiose and monumental arch to be reminded what a beautiful city Washington D.C. already is.

name: Nancy Dailey
text: I am against installing such a divisive project that will alter such a significant historical view during a year we are celebrating 250 years of American history. Please do not move forward with this project. A celebration of this type should be thought through and maybe mark paying off the national debt. It should be put in another location to not alter the excellent historic plan.

name: Richard Sparber

text: I strongly oppose the proposed Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. First, the monument would disrupt one of the most historically and symbolically important vistas in Washington, D.C. The visual corridor from Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House, across Memorial Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, is a carefully designed ceremonial landscape of profound national significance. Introducing a large triumphal arch into this setting would diminish the integrity, balance, and solemn character of this historic vista. Second, Memorial Circle is already one of the most complicated and heavily traveled traffic areas in the region. Southbound GW Parkway traffic merges with traffic coming from Memorial Bridge, Route 50 westbound, and northbound parkway traffic. Adding a monumental structure at this location would create an unnecessary distraction for commuters navigating an already difficult intersection, potentially increasing confusion and traffic accidents. Finally, Arlington National Cemetery does not need additional ornamentation. It is a hallowed burial ground for American military service members and their families. The cemetery should remain serene, peaceful, and respectful. A triumphal arch would detract from the solemnity of the landscape and introduce unnecessary political controversy into a place dedicated to remembrance, sacrifice, and national unity. This proposal appears to be a vanity project rather than an enhancement to the memorial landscape. The dignity and historic character of Arlington National Cemetery and Memorial Circle should be preserved without imposing a new monumental structure that conflicts with the purpose and spirit of the site. Respectfully submitted, Teri Bennett

name: Richard Stern
text: I would like to add my complete agreement with the following comment previously submitted: "May 20, 2026 Mr. Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., Chair U.S. Commission of Fine Arts 401 F Street, NW, Suite 312 Washington, DC 20001 Re: CFA 21/MAY/26-1 Memorial Circle, George Washington Memorial Parkway, Washington, DC. New Monumental Arch. Revised Concept. Dear Mr. Cook: The National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States ("National Trust") is a private charitable, educational, nonprofit corporation headquartered in Washington, D.C. and chartered by Congress in 1949 to further the historic preservation policy of the United States. 54 U.S.C. § 312102(a). This Congressional charter obligates the National Trust to "facilitate public participation in the preservation of sites, buildings, and objects of national significance or interest." We respectfully submit the following comments concerning the current proposal by the Executive Office of the President and the U.S. Department of the Interior to construct a new Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. We urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." We would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. After reviewing the revised concept plans that have been submitted to CFA, the National Trust remains concerned about the location, height, scale, and design of the proposed Triumphal Arch, the manner in which it interferes with existing commemorative works and fails to protect existing public uses and cultural resources. Notwithstanding comments and recommendations by Commission members at the April 2026 meeting, the modifications to the proposal have been minimal. Most notably, the 68-foot-high sculpture at the top of the proposed Arch has not been removed or reduced, contrary to the Commissioners' recommendation. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. The National Trust is also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission itself. We urge the Commission members to await the Section 106 process, which has not yet been initiated. Thank you for considering the views of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Sincerely, Carol Quillen President and Chief Executive Officer" Thank you, Richard Stern

text: I oppose the monumental arch based on the following key reasons: Obstructed Sightlines and Heritage: The 250-foot scale would dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and disrupt the historically solemn and carefully designed sightlines between the memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. name: Leslie Guidry
text: As a National Trust for Historic Preservation member, historic preservationist, and architectural historian, I agree with the National Trust's public comment in regard to the proposed monumental arch. Rules, regulations, and statutes need to be followed BEFORE to approval of the project. In the National Trust's own words: We urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." We would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress. After reviewing the revised concept plans that have been submitted to CFA, the National Trust remains concerned about the location, height, scale, and design of the proposed Triumphal Arch, the manner in which it interferes with existing commemorative works and fails to protect existing public uses and cultural resources. Notwithstanding comments and recommendations by Commission members at the April 2026 meeting, the modifications to the proposal have been minimal. Most notably, the 68-foot-high sculpture at the top of the proposed Arch has not been removed or reduced, contrary to the Commissioners' recommendation. The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. The National Trust is also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission itself. We urge the Commission members to await the Section 106 process, which has not yet been initiated.

text: I urge the Commission to reject the proposed Monumental Arch at Memorial Circle. The landscape itself is part of the memorial. The proposed arch would introduce a new dominant element into a carefully designed viewshed, altering a visual and symbolic relationship that has existed for generations. Once this change is made, it cannot be undone. I also believe the review process serves an important purpose. National memorial landscapes belong to the entire country. Decisions that permanently alter them should be approached with caution, broad public engagement, and deep respect for the historic design intent of these spaces. The existence of a formal review process reflects the understanding that preservation of nationally significant landscapes is a public responsibility. Future generations will inherit these places exactly as we leave them. In this case, preserving the existing landscape is the better choice.

name: Steven Rhodes
text: I am writing to submit formal comment regarding the design concept for the proposed New Monumental Arch at Memorial Circle. This submission addresses specific statutory, procedural, and logistical conflicts within the proposal that warrant a denial of concept approval by the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC). 1. Disruption of the Historic Viewshed and Spatial Planning The geographic corridor encompassing the Lincoln Memorial, the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington National Cemetery relies on a low-profile, horizontal axis deliberately established by the 1902 McMillan Plan. This design ensures an uninterrupted visual continuity across the Potomac River. Introducing a 250-foot vertical structure—more than double the height of the Lincoln Memorial—violates the established architectural hierarchy of the monumental core. Furthermore, the inclusion of internal elevators, commercial ticketing facilities, and private event spaces alters a landscape intended for public reflection into a managed commercial venue, fundamentally compromising the integrity of a protected national viewshed. 2. Statutory Non-Compliance under the Commemorative Works Act (40 U.S.C. § 8903) Because the proposed site on Columbia Island sits within Area I of the National Capital Core, the project is strictly bound by the Commemorative Works Act (CWA). The statute explicitly mandates independent legislative authorization from Congress for any such installation. Advancing design approvals through agency directives while bypassing direct congressional consent represents a clear statutory circumvention. Additionally, the inclusion of revenue-generating infrastructure, such as ticketing hubs and private galleries, is structurally incompatible with the preservation mandates governing this restricted civic zone. 3. Procedural Deficiencies under NHPA Section 106 The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) requires comprehensive Section 106 consultation to assess adverse effects on historic properties before physical implementation or final design approvals take place. Conducting preliminary site work and geotechnical surveying via existing corporate infrastructure contracts effectively fast-tracks physical execution before public and state historic preservation reviews are legally concluded, undermining the integrity of the administrative review process. 4. Logistical and Programmatic Incompatibility Memorial Circle functions as a critical traffic rotary managing high commuter volumes and solemn funeral processions entering Arlington National Cemetery. Introducing a high- occupancy observation platform and event venue at this specific junction creates unstudied vehicular chokepoints, transit delays, and pedestrian safety hazards on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. The National Capital Planning Commission should uphold its statutory mandate to protect the integrity of the monumental core and deny approval to this concept layout due to these outstanding statutory, procedural, and logistical conflicts.

name: Town of Roxbury Historic District Commission
text: To Whom It May Concern: This letter is to express our strong opposition to the proposal to construct a monumental arch on the National Mall at the direction of President Donald Trump. While we recognize the importance of commemorating national ideals and historic achievements, the proposed arch raises profound concerns regarding historical integrity, architectural harmony, and the stewardship of one of the nation's most prominent public spaces. The National Mall is not merely open land available for successive political monuments; it is a carefully planned historic landscape. Developed through the vision of Pierre L'Enfant and refined by the McMillan Commission Plan of 1901, the Mall reflects a coherent civic design rooted in democratic openness and visual continuity. The introduction of an oversized triumphal arch — particularly one associated with personal political legacy rather than broad national consensus — threatens to disrupt that carefully preserved framework. Historic preservationists are especially concerned that the proposed arch would undermine the visual relationships among existing monuments, memorials, and open vistas that define the Mall's character. The Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, Capitol dome, and reflecting pools were intentionally composed to create a sense of civic balance and national unity. A new monumental structure inserted into that composition risks overwhelming the existing design and altering the symbolic meaning of the space itself. There are also serious procedural concerns. Changes to federally protected historic landscapes traditionally require extensive public consultation, environmental review, and oversight by bodies such as the National Capital Planning Commission and the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. Preservation law exists precisely to prevent major alterations driven by transient political interests rather than enduring public consensus. The National Mall belongs to the American people across generations, not to any single administration. Furthermore, triumphal arches carry strong historical associations with imperial power, military conquest, and authoritarian self-celebration. Such symbolism is fundamentally at odds with the restrained democratic character of Washington's monumental core. America's civic architecture has historically favored memorials that invite reflection and shared remembrance rather than personal glorification or displays of dominance. Finally, preservationists believe public resources should prioritize maintaining and restoring the many existing historic structures and memorials already under strain from age, climate, and heavy tourism. The stewardship challenges facing the Mall today require conservation, not monumental expansion. For these reasons, we urge federal planners, preservation authorities, elected officials, and the public to reject the proposed arch and to uphold the historic integrity of the National Mall for future generations. Sincerely, Roxbury, CT Historic District Commission Attachment

name: Rebecca A. Fellerman
text: As an architect with over 30 years experience, and a former resident of DC, I respectfully recommend that the committee refuse approval of the proposed memorial arch. As noted by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House. I am also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial. In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers. Respectfully Submitted, Rebecca A. Fellerman, AIA, NCARB, RA

name: Cathy Koch
text: We write to express our strong opposition to the proposed 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" slated for Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, and to urge the National Trust to continue its principled advocacy against this deeply misguided project. Arlington National Cemetery is not a backdrop — it is consecrated ground. More than 400,000 of America's fallen service members are buried there. The solemn visual corridor connecting the Lincoln Memorial across the Arlington Memorial Bridge to those hallowed acres has stood for over a century as one of the most meaningful and carefully preserved viewsheds in the entire nation. To erect a 250-foot structure — taller than the Arc de Triomphe by nearly 100 feet — at the very entrance to that sacred space is an act of profound disrespect to the dead and to the living who mourn them. This proposal bypassed the deliberate, congressionally mandated processes that exist precisely to protect such irreplaceable landscapes. The public has spoken overwhelmingly: at a recent Commission of Fine Arts hearing, 99.5% of over 600 submitted public comments opposed the structure. Vietnam War veterans have gone to federal court to stop it. Members of Congress have introduced legislation to block it permanently. The voice of the American people on this matter could not be clearer. The National Trust's own stated concerns — that the arch's scale and placement will dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and overwhelm the ceremonial entrance to Arlington — are exactly right. No anniversary celebration, however well-intentioned, justifies permanently altering one of America's most spiritually significant landscapes. There are countless ways to honor 250 years of American independence that do not require bulldozing history and the dignity of the dead. We urge the National Trust to: 1. Submit forceful written comments to the National Capital Planning Commission ahead of the June 3, 2026 deadline opposing this project. 2. Continue coordinating with veterans' organizations, preservation advocates, and congressional allies to halt construction. 3. Pursue all available legal and regulatory avenues to ensure that no structure of this kind is erected without full congressional authorization and genuine public consent. The integrity of our national memory is not a bargaining chip. We are grateful for the National Trust's leadership on this issue and urge you to hold the line. Respectfully, Cathy and James Koch cathykoch7@gmail.com (630) 244-1486

name: Gerritt and Elizabeth Baker-Smith
text: We are writing with much concern - and yes, a degree of horror and disgust - at the President's plan to build a huge, domineering arch inbetween the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States ("National Trust") is a private charitable, educational, nonprofit corporation headquartered in Washington, D.C. and chartered by Congress in 1949 to further the historic preservation policy of the United States. 54 U.S.C. § 312102(a). The National Trust(chartered by Congress in 1949) with a specific duty to "facilitate public participation in the preservation of sites, buildings, and objects of national significance or interest."We are adding our voices to their comments respectfully submitted comments concerning the current proposal by the Executive Office of the President and the U.S. Department of the Interior to construct a new Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. We urge the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts ("CFA") to consider these comments in connection with its responsibility under the Commemorative Works Act, following consultation with the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, to approve site and design proposals for commemorative works so that such works do not "interfere with, or encroach on, an existing commemorative work and to the maximum extent practicable, protect open space, existing public use, and cultural and natural resources." We would also remind the members of the CFA that the Commemorative Works Act requires the project to be approved by Congress.After reviewing the revised concept plans that have been submitted to CFA, the National Trust remains concerned about the location, height, scale, and design of the proposed Triumphal Arch, the manner in which it interferes with existing commemorative works and fails to protect existing public uses and cultural resources. Notwithstanding comments and recommendations by Commission members at the April 2026 meeting, the modifications to the proposal have been minimal. Most notably, the 68-foot-high sculpture at the top of the proposed Arch has not been removed or reduced, contrary to the Commissioners' recommendation.The location of the proposed Arch, at Memorial Circle, will interrupt the highly significant relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. One of the most symbolic landscape vistas in Washington, DC, the vista was designed to represent the post-Civil War reconciliation of the north and south of the United States. Arlington Memorial Bridge was intentionally designed with a low profile to respect the visual and symbolic vistas connecting the National Mall and National Cemetery. If constructed as planned at the proposed location, the new Triumphal Arch will obscure the intentional axial and aesthetic relationships between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington Memorial Bridge, and Arlington House.The National Trust is also deeply concerned about the unprecedented height and scale of the proposed Triumphal Arch, which will overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House. The proposed Arch would be double the size of the Lincoln Memorial and would risk disrespecting this powerful and beloved monument. As such, the Triumphal Arch is inconsistent with the McMillan Plan and subsequent planning decisions that have stewarded the National Mall as a unified composition characterized by long, open, and uninterrupted viewsheds, with a clear hierarchy of monumental elements, that culminates at its western end at the Lincoln Memorial.In addition, the proposed location of the Arch, at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, is inconsistent with the solemn historic character of Arlington National Cemetery. The hallowed resting place of 400,000 veterans and their families, Arlington National Cemetery is a powerful reminder of American military sacrifice, selfless service, and national unity, all within sight of the monumental core of the Nation's Capital. Distinguished by the Tomb of the Unknowns, Memorial Avenue, and rolling hillsides of uniform rows of simple headstones, Arlington National Cemetery is a living memorial that honors thirty funeral services each day. The Arch, as proposed, would dominate Arlington National Cemetery, and be inconsistent with its hallowed character of solemn graves with powerful, unadorned white markers.Finally, it is important to note that review of the proposal under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has not yet been initiated. We understand that the National Park Service will be initiating Section 106 consultation soon, but the statute mandates that the review process be completed "prior to" approval of the project. 54 U.S.C. § 306108. In addition, based on past experience with Section 106 consultation in the National Capitol region, the proposed plans will be improved in response to the collaborative review and comments from the expert professional staff of the involved agencies, including the Commission itself. We urge the Commission members to await the Section 106 process, which has not yet been initiated. Thank you for your consideration.

text: Gloria Johnson 442 Oyster Drive La Selva Beach, CA 95076 May 28, 2026 National Capital Planning Commission 401 9th Street, NW, Suite 500 Washington, DC 20004 Re: Concerns Regarding the Proposed Monumental Arch** Dear Members of the Commission, I am writing to express serious concerns about the proposed Monumental Arch and its impact on the integrity of the National Mall and its surrounding memorials. While I appreciate the desire to honor American achievement, I believe this project, as currently designed, would cause lasting harm to one of our most sacred civic landscapes. **The Arch Would Overwhelm the Lincoln Memorial** The Lincoln Memorial stands as one of the most beloved and architecturally significant structures in the United States. Its scale and setting were carefully conceived to convey solemnity, humility, and the weight of Lincoln's legacy. A monumental arch of the proposed dimensions would dwarf this iconic structure, fundamentally disrupting the visual hierarchy of the Mall and diminishing the memorial's presence in the landscape. No new construction should subordinate a monument of such historical and emotional importance to the American people. **The View Corridor to Arlington National Cemetery Must Be Protected** The sightline from the Lincoln Memorial across the Potomac to Arlington National Cemetery is not merely scenic — it is deeply symbolic. It connects the president who preserved the Union with the ground where soldiers of that same Union are laid to rest. This view represents the nation's long and difficult journey toward healing after the Civil War. To obstruct it with a new structure would sever a meaningful and irreplaceable visual and historical bond that Americans have honored for over a century. **The Design Elements Are Inappropriate for This Setting** I must also raise concern about the reported gold statuary proposed for the top of the arch. The memorials of the National Mall share a common language of restraint, dignity, and timelessness. Gilded statues would strike a discordant note entirely out of keeping with this tradition, and would risk reducing a solemn civic space to spectacle. The Mall deserves design choices that will be respected and cherished by future generations, not ones that prioritize visual extravagance over meaning. I urge the Commission to carefully weigh these concerns and to prioritize the preservation of the Mall's character, its historic view corridors, and the dignity of its existing memorials. I would welcome the opportunity to provide further comment during the public review process. Thank you for your consideration. Respectfully, Gloria Johnson johnsontierney@gmail.com (408) 218-7367
